questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain where fungal digestion occurs before nutrients are taken up.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-4021 asks why a mould colony spreads over a stale slice of bread rather than feeding on its surface.

options.text: It secretes enzymes onto the bread and then absorbs the soluble products of digestion
It engulfs crumb particles whole and digests them inside a gut cavity
options.misconception: believes fungi swallow solid food and digest it internally

options.text: It captures light reflected from the crust and fixes carbon by photosynthesis
options.misconception: confuses fungi with photosynthetic autotrophs

options.text: It absorbs whole crumb particles through the hyphae into the cytoplasm
options.misconception: thinks hyphae take up solid particles without enzymes

questions.explanation: Fungi secrete enzymes onto the substrate, digesting food outside the cell, then absorb the soluble products. Swallowing food or absorbing whole crumbs are animal strategies.
questions.hint: Consider where the digestive enzymes are released.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the nutritional role played by a saprotrophic fungus in an ecosystem.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-4188 notes that fallen logs in a damp forest are colonised by white fungal threads.

options.text: The fungus gains carbon by parasitising living tree roots beneath the log
options.misconception: confuses a saprotroph with a parasitic or mutualistic fungus

options.text: The fungus gains carbon by digesting dead organic matter with secreted enzymes
The fungus gains carbon by taking up mineral salts released by weathering rock
options.misconception: assumes fungi feed on inorganic minerals like chemotrophs

options.text: The fungus gains carbon by photosynthesis using the faint forest light
options.misconception: claims fungi carry out photosynthesis in dim woodland

questions.explanation: A saprotroph lives on dead organic matter, secreting enzymes to release soluble nutrients which it then absorbs. It neither attacks living tissue, nor mines minerals, nor photosynthesises.
questions.hint: Think about where the fungus obtains its carbon.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an obligate parasite from a facultative one using evidence from a culture experiment.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-5150 reports that a rust-coloured fungus grew on a living wheat leaf but failed to grow on any agar plate.

options.text: The fungus is a facultative parasite because it grows well without a host
options.misconception: reads failure on agar as proof of facultative growth

options.text: The fungus is a saprotroph because it cannot grow on dead material alone
options.misconception: treats inability to grow on agar as proof of saprotrophy

options.text: The fungus is an obligate parasite because it grows only on living host tissue
The fungus is a free-living decomposer that infects the leaf by accident
options.misconception: assumes accidental infection makes it a decomposer

questions.explanation: Growth only on living host tissue with no growth on nutrient-rich agar shows the fungus cannot complete its life cycle alone. An obligate parasite depends on living host cells for nutrients.
questions.hint: What does the absence of growth on agar prove?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The cell wall as a drug target
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate why a drug that blocks fungal wall synthesis spares human cells.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-6203 flags a report claiming a new antifungal works because it dissolves fungal membranes.

options.text: The claim is wrong because human cells also contain a rigid cell wall
options.misconception: thinks human cells possess a chitinous wall

options.text: The claim is wrong because fungal walls contain no material a drug could bind
options.misconception: assumes fungal walls are chemically featureless

options.text: The claim is wrong because membrane drugs act on cholesterol found in animals
options.misconception: claims animal cholesterol is the target of all antifungals

options.text: The claim is wrong because human cells lack the chitin and glucan wall polymers

questions.explanation: Fungal walls are built from chitin and glucans that human cells lack, so blocking their synthesis spares host cells. Membranes are a different target, and human cells carry cholesterol.
questions.hint: Which polymers are unique to fungal walls?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether a compound disrupts fungal membrane sterols.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-7742 asks for a laboratory test of a suspected polyene antifungal before it is screened further.

answer.exemplar: Grow two identical broth cultures of the same yeast strain, add the compound to one at a range of concentrations and add an equal volume of solvent to the other. Measure growth rate and leakage of cell contents through the membrane, and include a known polyene as a positive control. If treated cells lyse and leak while the solvent control grows normally, the compound is disrupting membrane sterols.

questions.explanation: A good design varies the compound concentration and includes an untreated and a positive control. That way membrane damage can be attributed to sterol disruption rather than to the solvent.
questions.hint: Include an untreated control and a known active drug.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single dilution cannot give an accurate count of a dense culture.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-8809 explains that a student plated an undiluted overnight broth and counted a continuous lawn.

answer.exemplar: When a sample is plated undiluted, cells are far too crowded to resolve into separate colonies, so counting is impossible and any estimate is meaningless. Serial dilution spreads the cells over a wide range of plates, and a plate in the countable range gives a reliable figure that can be scaled back to the original density.

questions.explanation: Too many cells merge into a lawn, so no count can be taken. A series of dilutions produces at least one plate with separated colonies that can be counted and scaled back.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when cells are too crowded.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The countable range on a plate
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the original cell density from colonies on a plate of known dilution.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-9114 states that 0.1 millilitres of a ten to the minus six dilution was plated and gave 24 separate colonies.
questions.explanation: The plate counts cells from 0.1 millilitres of a one in a million dilution, so the original holds 24 divided by 0.1 times a million per millilitre. That is 240 million cells per millilitre.
questions.hint: Divide colonies by the volume plated and the dilution.

questions.topic: Counting cells on a counting chamber
questions.learningObjective: Apply a two-step method to estimate a cell suspension density using a counting chamber.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-9446 asks how a technician proceeds when a suspension of yeast cells must be counted today.

options.text: Count the cells in five squares, then divide by the volume counted and the dilution factor
Count the cells in five squares, then multiply by the volume counted and the dilution factor
options.misconception: multiplies by the dilution instead of dividing by it

options.text: Count the cells in one square and multiply by the chamber depth and the dilution factor
options.misconception: ignores the volume of the squares actually counted

options.text: Count the cells on the whole slide and divide by the volume counted and the dilution factor
options.misconception: counts outside the ruled area and dilutes the estimate

questions.explanation: The mean count per square becomes cells per millilitre by dividing by the volume of the squares counted, then dividing again for any dilution. Multiplying by the dilution would inflate the estimate.
questions.hint: Remember to correct for any dilution of the sample.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about why absorption rather than ingestion suits a filamentous body plan.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1055 argues that the branching hyphal shape suits absorptive feeding better than a tubular gut does.

options.text: Hyphae grow towards nutrient patches so the whole surface can secrete and absorb enzymes
options.misconception: treats branching as a way of swallowing larger food pieces

options.text: Hyphae grow towards nutrient patches, so their tips can secrete enzymes and absorb products
Hyphae carry food along their length to a central stomach chamber for digestion
options.misconception: imagines a central digestive organ inside the fungal body

options.text: Hyphae pump food particles inward through pores in the cell wall into the cytoplasm
options.misconception: believes cell walls contain valves for importing solid food

questions.explanation: A branching filament spreads its absorbing surface through the substrate, with growing tips secreting enzymes and taking up the products released. Fungi have no gut or stomach.
questions.hint: Focus on what the growing tip of a hypha actually does.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a saprotroph contributes to nutrient cycling in a woodland.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1211 describes a compost heap in which heat and mushroom fruit bodies appear over several weeks.

options.text: Saprotrophs trap carbon from the air and add it to the heap as they grow
options.misconception: claims decomposers fix atmospheric carbon by photosynthesis

options.text: Saprotrophs convert dead material directly into mineral salts inside their cells
options.misconception: believes digestion happens inside a fungal digestive tract

options.text: Saprotrophs release carbon locked in dead material back into the ecosystem as they digest it
Saprotrophs remove carbon from dead material and store it permanently in their bodies
options.misconception: assumes fungal carbon is permanently locked away in the heap

questions.explanation: Saprotrophs secrete enzymes into dead material, absorb the released organic compounds and respire much of the carbon back as carbon dioxide. Their role returns nutrients to the ecosystem.
questions.hint: Think about the carbon dioxide released during respiration.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse host specificity data to distinguish a parasite from a saprotroph.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1377 reports that a fungus grows on living bean plants, dies on cut beans in a dish, and never grows on agar.

options.text: The organism is a saprotroph because it fails on any medium without a plant
options.misconception: reads failure on dead tissue as proof of saprotrophy

options.text: The organism is a free-living decomposer with an unusual temperature requirement
options.misconception: invokes a growth condition instead of host dependence

options.text: The organism is a saprotroph that happens to grow better on living bean tissue
options.misconception: claims preference for living tissue proves saprotrophy

options.text: The organism is an obligate biotroph that takes nutrients from living host cells

questions.explanation: Growth on living plants with no growth on dead tissue or agar shows the fungus needs living host cells, the hallmark of an obligate biotroph. A saprotroph would grow on plain agar.
questions.hint: Compare growth on living and dead material.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The cell wall as a drug target
questions.learningObjective: Detect a faulty claim about fungal walls in a customer support answer.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1490 records a chatbot answering that antifungal drugs work by preventing humans from building cell walls.

options.text: The answer wrongly implies humans have cell walls for the drug to block
The answer wrongly implies the drug attacks bacterial rather than fungal walls
options.misconception: confuses fungal walls with bacterial peptidoglycan

options.text: The answer is correct because both fungal and human cells secrete a wall matrix
options.misconception: believes human cells secrete an extracellular wall matrix

options.text: The answer wrongly implies fungal walls contain no chitin at all
options.misconception: claims fungal walls are made entirely of glucans

questions.explanation: Human cells have no cell wall, so the drug cannot be blocking human wall synthesis. Fungal walls contain chitin and glucans, and humans lack the enzymes needed to build them.
questions.hint: Check the claim about human cell structure.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Plan a comparison of two azole drugs on fungal growth.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1622 requests an experiment comparing two azole antifungal agents against the same mould strain.

answer.exemplar: Set up matched broth cultures of the same mould strain, one with drug A, one with drug B and one with no drug, each at several concentrations, and keep inoculum and incubation time identical. Measure turbidity or dry mass to compare growth, include a solvent control, and repeat the series to check consistency. Any difference in the concentration needed to halt growth shows a difference in potency.

questions.explanation: Holding strain, inoculum and incubation constant isolates the effect of each drug, while several concentrations and a solvent control reveal potency. Replication guards against a misleading result.
questions.hint: Change only the drug and hold everything else constant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a dilution series is prepared and why the order of steps matters.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-1788 asks a new laboratory assistant to describe how tenfold dilutions should be carried out safely.

answer.exemplar: A fresh sterile pipette is used for each dilution and the tip is changed between tubes, because a single reused pipette carries cells forward and inflates the count. A measured volume is transferred into fresh diluent and mixed well before the next step, so the sample is homogeneous. Always take from the mixed tube and dilute towards the end of the series.

questions.explanation: Using a fresh pipette for each step prevents carry-over of cells between dilutions, which would make later plates too crowded. Thorough mixing keeps the sample homogeneous.
questions.hint: Think about what a reused pipette would transfer.

questions.explanation: The fungus gained 0.36 grams of new biomass from 0.50 grams of substrate, which is 0.72 or 72 percent of the substrate converted into fungal dry mass. The remainder was respired or lost as waste.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Counting cells on a counting chamber
questions.learningObjective: Choose a chamber dilution so that cells fall in a countable range.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2044 asks which dilution of a crowded yeast suspension should be loaded onto the counting chamber.

options.text: Dilute so that roughly thirty cells are visible per ruled square, then count
options.misconception: aims for a dense field where cells overlap

options.text: Dilute so that about five to twenty cells lie in each ruled square, then count
Dilute so that no cells appear, since an empty square is easier to count
options.misconception: believes an empty ruled square gives a valid estimate

options.text: Load the undiluted sample so that the full population is represented exactly
options.misconception: assumes an undiluted load avoids sampling error entirely

questions.explanation: A workable count needs enough cells in the ruled area to be statistically useful but few enough that they are separate, typically five to twenty per square. Overcrowding or empty squares both mislead.
questions.hint: Aim for a cell number per square that is easy to resolve.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a fungal feature is consistent with absorptive nutrition.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2180 asks whether the observation of a fungus growing only where a breadcrumb fell supports absorptive nutrition.

options.text: No, because growth confined to crumbs shows the fungus needs light to feed
options.misconception: links restricted growth to a light requirement

options.text: No, because a fungus cannot use starch at all in its nutrition
options.misconception: assumes fungi cannot digest plant polysaccharides

options.text: Yes, because growth follows the organic substrate that supplies absorbable nutrients
Yes, because restricted growth proves the fungus absorbs molecules through its cell wall
options.misconception: claims the wall itself performs nutrient uptake

questions.explanation: Fungal growth follows where organic matter is available, which is what an absorptive heterotroph does when it digests substrate externally and takes up the products. Light has no role here.
questions.hint: Follow the carbon source rather than the light.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why obligate parasites make poor laboratory model organisms.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2319 notes that a rust fungus cannot be grown in a jar of nutrient broth alone.

options.text: Because the spores need light and warmth rather than nutrients to germinate
options.misconception: credits a physical condition instead of host nutrients

options.text: Because the spores are too fragile to survive being transferred to broth
options.misconception: blames handling rather than nutritional dependence

options.text: Because the fungus needs the correct pH of soil rather than a laboratory medium
options.misconception: assumes soil conditions matter more than a host

options.text: Because the spores require carbon from living host tissue to complete germination

questions.explanation: An obligate parasite takes nutrients from living host cells, so plain broth cannot support it. Light, handling and pH may affect growth but do not replace the living host as the carbon source.

questions.topic: The cell wall as a drug target
questions.learningObjective: Interpret data showing a fungal-specific enzyme inhibited by a candidate drug.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2456 reports that a candidate drug stops fungal growth but leaves human cell cultures dividing normally.

options.text: The drug most likely inhibits a fungal wall enzyme that human cells lack
The drug most likely blocks human DNA synthesis but spares fungal DNA
options.misconception: reverses the likely target between host and fungus

options.text: The drug most likely dissolves fungal membranes but not human ones
options.misconception: jumps to a membrane explanation without evidence

options.text: The drug most likely blocks fungal ribosomes at a site human ribosomes lack
options.misconception: assumes fungal ribosomes differ enough to spare human cells

questions.explanation: Selective toxicity points to a target in fungi but absent from human cells, and fungal wall enzymes fit. Human ribosomes resemble fungal ones, and both membranes hold similar lipids.
questions.hint: Look for a target that humans simply do not have.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify an error in a claim that an antifungal works by blocking protein synthesis.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2598 rejects a draft answer saying polyene drugs stop fungi by blocking ribosome movement along messenger RNA.

options.text: The draft is wrong because fungi have no ribosomes of any kind
options.misconception: denies that fungal cells translate proteins

options.text: The draft is wrong because polyenes bind membrane sterols and create pores
The draft is wrong because ribosome blocking occurs in plant chloroplasts alone
options.misconception: confuses fungal protein synthesis with plant organelles

options.text: The draft is wrong because the true target is the fungal cell wall polysaccharide
options.misconception: switches the mechanism to the wall instead of the membrane

questions.explanation: Polyene drugs act on the membrane, binding to ergosterol and forming pores that leak cell contents. They do not touch ribosomes, and fungal walls are the target of a different drug class.
questions.hint: Recall what polyenes do to ergosterol.

questions.learningObjective: Compute how much more drug a resistant strain needs compared with a sensitive one.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2703 states that complete inhibition needs 8 micrograms per millilitre for a sensitive yeast and 32 for a resistant strain.
questions.explanation: The resistant strain requires 32 divided by 8, that is four times the concentration of the sensitive strain before growth stops. A ratio that size indicates reduced drug sensitivity.
questions.hint: Divide the resistant concentration by the sensitive one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a duplicate plate improves confidence in a colony count.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2841 asks why the protocol plates two identical dilutions of the same sample rather than one.

answer.exemplar: Plating the same dilution twice gives two independent counts from the same original sample, so agreement between them shows the result is reproducible while disagreement reveals random error in pipetting, mixing or colony counting. The mean of agreeing counts is a better estimate than a single count, and the spread between plates indicates the precision achieved.

questions.explanation: Duplicate plates turn a single reading into two independent readings, which exposes random error and allows a mean to be taken when they agree. A single plate gives no measure of uncertainty.
questions.hint: Two readings let you check reproducibility.

questions.stem: Ticket BIO-2977 gives plate counts of 320 colonies at ten to the minus five, 45 at ten to the minus six and 3 at ten to the minus seven.

options.misconception: counts a plate that carries too many colonies

options.text: The 10^-7 plate is the best choice, giving 30 colonies per millilitre of that dilution
options.misconception: counts a plate below the reliable range

options.text: The 10^-6 plate is the best choice, giving 450 colonies per millilitre of that dilution
None of the three plates is usable, so the density must be reported as undetermined
options.misconception: assumes no plate can ever be counted

questions.explanation: Only the 10^-6 plate falls inside the reliable range of thirty to three hundred colonies. Its forty-five colonies equal 45 divided by 0.1 millilitres, that is 450 per millilitre of that dilution.
questions.hint: Pick the plate with thirty to three hundred colonies.

questions.stem: Ticket BIO-3055 lists the steps a student should follow to obtain a yeast count from a chamber slide.

options.text: Load the chamber first, mix the suspension afterwards, then count in known squares
options.misconception: loads the sample before resuspending the settled cells

options.text: Count in the squares first, then mix the suspension and reload the same chamber

options.misconception: counts the cells before they have settled into one plane

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Outline a broth dilution assay for a candidate antifungal.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-3563 asks the team to draft a method for finding the minimum concentration of a new drug that stops a mould.

answer.exemplar: Prepare a series of broth tubes containing the drug at a range of concentrations, plus a tube with solvent only as a control, and inoculate each with the same volume of the same mould spore suspension. Incubate all tubes under identical conditions and read them for visible growth or turbidity. The lowest concentration with no growth is the minimum inhibitory concentration, and each test should be repeated to check the result is reliable.

questions.explanation: A broth dilution assay needs a range of concentrations, a growth control and identical inoculum in every tube. The lowest concentration that stops growth is the minimum inhibitory concentration.
questions.hint: Vary concentration only and keep all other variables equal.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why diluent in the tubes must be sterile and why the first tube is discarded.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-3648 asks why the first dilution tube may be set aside before plating the series.

answer.exemplar: Non-sterile diluent would introduce stray microorganisms that form colonies of their own, so the counted colonies would no longer belong to the sample. The first tube often receives the largest transfer volume and most handling, so its count is the least reliable. Discarding it and counting from later dilutions reduces both contamination risk and sampling error.

questions.explanation: Sterile diluent stops contamination colonies being counted as sample cells, and the first tube, which takes most handling, is least representative. Later dilutions give cleaner counts.
questions.hint: Consider what stray microbes would do to the count.

questions.topic: Counting cells on a counting chamber
questions.learningObjective: Decide which chamber squares should be counted for a reliable estimate.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-3899 asks which of four counting squares should contribute to a yeast density estimate.

options.text: Count the two squares with the most cells, since they give the largest sample
options.misconception: chooses squares by high count rather than by rule

options.text: Count the square nearest the edge where the cells have settled

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design a control to show that a drug kills fungi rather than merely slowing them.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-4352 asks how to show that a membrane-active compound kills fungal cells and not only arrests their division.

answer.exemplar: Treat matched cultures with the compound and with solvent alone, then wash the cells and transfer them to fresh drug-free medium. If treated cells fail to resume growth after the drug is removed while control cells grow normally, the compound is fungicidal. Measuring the proportion of cells able to form colonies after treatment gives a quantitative measure of killing.

questions.explanation: Telling killing from inhibition requires removing the drug and seeing whether growth resumes, because inhibited cells recover and killed cells do not. A solvent control makes this measurable.
questions.hint: Remove the drug and ask whether growth resumes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of plating more than one dilution in a serial dilution series.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-4467 asks why the laboratory protocol spreads several dilutions of one sample across separate plates.

answer.exemplar: A single dilution can easily miss the useful range, giving either a confluent lawn or too few isolated colonies to count. Spreading several dilutions means at least one plate will fall in the countable range of roughly thirty to three hundred colonies, whatever the original density of the sample. The unused plates also allow the density to be checked against two independent dilutions.

questions.explanation: Unknown densities make one dilution unreliable, so a series guarantees at least one plate in the countable range and allows a cross-check. A single plate risks a lawn or a count too low.
questions.hint: One dilution may land outside the countable range.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Propose an explanation for why polyene drugs are toxic to a patient.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-5151 asks the team to explain and test why a patient on a polyene drug became jaundiced.

answer.exemplar: Polyenes bind ergosterol but also have some affinity for human cholesterol, which is concentrated in cell membranes, including those of liver cells. Disruption of liver cell membranes could cause leakage and jaundice. This can be tested by measuring membrane leakage and liver enzyme release in human liver cells exposed to the drug, compared with untreated cells, and by assaying how much drug binds human cholesterol relative to ergosterol.

questions.explanation: Polyenes may not be wholly specific for ergosterol and could also damage human membranes, especially in the liver. Testing leakage and binding to human cholesterol would check that idea.
questions.hint: Compare binding to human cholesterol and to ergosterol.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Justify a sample volume of 0.1 millilitres for spread plating.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-5264 asks why spread plating uses a small known volume rather than a large one.

answer.exemplar: A small known volume keeps the number of cells landing on each plate within the countable range and gives an exact divisor when scaling the count back to the original density. A larger volume would deposit too many cells, producing a lawn that cannot be counted. It also spreads more evenly, so colonies stay separate and can be attributed to single cells.

questions.explanation: The volume plated must be known exactly because it divides the count, and it must be small enough to avoid a lawn. A larger volume improves nothing and usually ruins the plate.
questions.hint: The volume plated is the divisor in the final calculation.

options.misconception: overshoots the dilution and leaves too few cells to count

options.text: Plate the undiluted broth, which spreads about 25000 cells onto the plate

options.misconception: picks too shallow a dilution and crowds the plate

options.text: Plate a ten to the minus two dilution, which spreads about 250 cells onto the plate

questions.hint: Work out how many cells 0.1 millilitres would deliver.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Counting cells on a counting chamber
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a haemocytometer yields a cell density per millilitre.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-5483 asks a new analyst to describe how a haemocytometer result is turned into cells per millilitre.

answer.exemplar: The chamber has a known volume beneath each ruled square, so the number of cells counted can be divided by that volume to give a concentration in that ruled area. Multiplying by the known chamber depth converts the count into a concentration for the whole chamber, and multiplying by ten to the six converts the chamber volume into a millilitre. Any dilution of the sample must finally be divided out.

questions.explanation: Chamber geometry supplies the calibration, so a count in known squares becomes a concentration once depth and volume are applied, then divided by any dilution. Without that it stays per square.
questions.hint: Use the known chamber volume, then correct for dilution.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment comparing drug effect on membrane integrity and cell survival.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-5974 requests an experiment measuring how a membrane-targeting drug affects fungal cell integrity.

answer.exemplar: Expose matched cultures to the drug at several concentrations for a fixed time, then measure leakage of a cytoplasmic marker such as potassium or a coloured dye into the medium, alongside a colony count on drug-free recovery plates. Include untreated and solvent controls. Increasing leakage together with a falling colony count shows the drug is damaging membranes and killing cells rather than merely slowing their growth.

questions.explanation: Measuring membrane leakage and the ability to form colonies distinguishes damage from slowing, while doses and controls tie the result to the drug. One reading cannot tell killing from inhibition.
questions.hint: Measure both leakage and survival after drug removal.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of using the same pipette for every dilution step.
questions.stem: Ticket BIO-6073 asks why a student who used one pipette throughout produced wildly inconsistent plate counts.

answer.exemplar: A pipette reused from tube to tube carries a film of the previous, more concentrated sample into the next tube. Each dilution then receives extra cells, so the count no longer represents a true tenfold dilution and later plates are far too crowded. Using a fresh sterile pipette, or rinsing with the new diluent, removes the carry-over and restores the expected tenfold steps.

questions.explanation: Carry-over of concentrated cells inflates every subsequent dilution, breaking the tenfold series and producing inconsistent counts. A fresh pipette per step, or thorough rinsing, removes the error.
questions.hint: Think about what the pipette carries between tubes.
